Holyday
hō'li-dā
n. (a religious festival day; in Psalm 42 remembered with longing, and in Colossians named among the shadows fulfilled in Christ)
From holy and day, and the ancestor of the modern holiday — a drift that records what happened to the institution. In Colossians 2:16 it renders Greek heorte, a feast.

Biblical Definition

The Psalmist, in exile from the sanctuary, remembers what he has lost: “When I remember these things, I pour out my soul in me: for I had gone with the multitude, I went with them to the house of God, with the voice of joy and praise, with a multitude that kept holyday” (Psalm 42:4). What he misses is corporate — the multitude, the going with them, the voice of joy and praise — and the memory of it is what makes his present thirst so sharp. Paul uses the word in his warning against those who would bind the Colossians to the ceremonial calendar: “Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days” (Colossians 2:16). The ground is given in the next verse and it is Christological, not indifferentist: these things “are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ” (Colossians 2:17). The feasts were not empty; they were shadows cast by a body that has now arrived. A man who returns to the shadow after the body has come is not more devout, and no one may judge a believer for declining to.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines holyday as a day set apart for commemorating some important event, a religious anniversary, and notes its use for a day of joy and gaiety.

expand to see more

HOLYDAY, n. A day set apart for commemorating some important event; an anniversary consecrated to religious observance.

2. A day of joy and gaiety.

3. A day of exemption from labor; a day of amusement.

FESTIVAL, n. The time of feasting; an anniversary day of joy, civil or religious.

SHADOW, n. A representation of something made by light; hence, an imperfect and faint representation, opposed to substance.

Key Scripture

Psalm 42:4 — "When I remember these things, I pour out my soul in me: for I had gone with the multitude, I went with them to the house of God, with the voice of joy and praise, with a multitude that kept holyday."

Colossians 2:16 — "Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days:"

Colossians 2:17 — "Which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ."

Leviticus 23:39 — "Also in the fifteenth day of the seventh month, when ye have gathered in the fruit of the land, ye shall keep a feast unto the LORD seven days: on the first day shall be a sabbath, and on the eighth day shall be a sabbath."

Modern Corruption

The word's own history tells the story: a holy day became a holiday, and the day off outlived the thing it was for.

expand to see more

Holyday and holiday are the same word, and the split between them is a record of what the culture did with the institution. The day was set apart for God, then set apart from work, then simply set apart for the self. Every major Christian observance in the West has completed some portion of that journey. The remedy is not the recovery of a crowded liturgical calendar, which Colossians 2:16 expressly refuses to impose; it is the recovery of the one day God has appointed for His church — the Lord's Day — as a day of worship rather than a slot of leisure. The regulative principle bears directly here: what God has commanded for corporate worship is required, and what He has not commanded may not be bound on the conscience.

Colossians 2:16 is misused in both directions. Some quote it to prove that all days are alike and therefore that no day is to be kept, which ignores that the Lord's Day is the settled practice of the New Testament church and confessed as the Christian sabbath. Others ignore it entirely and rebuild the ceremonial calendar as a mark of seriousness. Paul's argument is against neither observance nor liberty as such but against judging a brother over the shadows, since the body is of Christ. Psalm 42:4 supplies the pastoral counterweight to all such disputes: what the exile longed for was not the calendar but the multitude, the house of God, and the voice of joy and praise.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek heorte (G1859), a feast — Colossians 2:16; skia (G4639), a shadow — Colossians 2:17; Hebrew chagag, to keep festival — Psalm 42:4.

expand to see more

Greek heorte (G1859) — a festival; Colossians 2:16, and used throughout the Gospels of the Jewish feasts.

Greek skia (G4639) — a shadow; Colossians 2:17, Hebrews 8:5, Hebrews 10:1 — the shadow implies a body casting it.

Greek soma (G4983) — body, substance; Colossians 2:17, set against the shadow.

Hebrew chagag — to keep a pilgrim feast; Psalm 42:4, of the multitude that kept holyday.

Hebrews 10:1 states the same principle: the law having a shadow of good things to come, and not the very image of the things.

Usage

"“With a multitude that kept holyday” — what the exile missed was the multitude."

"“Let no man therefore judge you… in respect of an holyday” — the shadow may not bind the conscience."

"“The body is of Christ” — the shadows were cast by something real."
